title: Anode-free configurations through separator-mediated interfacial regulation for practical sodium metal batteries
content: Separator-mediated interfacial regulation has emerged as a central design principle for enabling high-performance sodium metal batteries, particularly in anode-free configurations where reversibility must be achieved without excess sodium. This Review outlines how functionally engineered separators, rather than acting as passive barriers, can regulate Na+ transport, homogenize ion flux, stabilize the solid–electrolyte interphase, and suppress dendritic growth under increasingly stringent operating conditions. We discuss the interfacial origins of failure in conventional and anode-free sodium metal batteries, define the key physicochemical requirements of separators, and survey passive and functional architectures across structural, chemical, and bio-derived design spaces. We pay special attention to separator strategies that couple mechanical adaptation with solvation control and field-assisted ion regulation, reconciling rapid transport with interfacial stability. Finally, we highlight emerging separator concepts for anode-free systems and identify the major challenges that remain for practical deployment, including scalability, durability, and validation under realistic cell conditions. Together, these advances establish separators as active interfacial regulators and point to a broadly applicable pathway toward safer, higher-energy sodium metal batteries.
